source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ τὰ μὲν ἡμέτερα περὶ ἀναστάσεως, ὡς ἐνεχώρει, ἀπὸ τοῦ μέρους ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος λέλεκται (συντέτακται γὰρ ἡμῖν περὶ ἀναστάσεως ἐν ἄλλοις, ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐξετάσασι τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον). τὰ δὲ τοῦ Κέλσου νῦν χρὴ κατὰ τὸ εὔλογον διαλαβεῖν, μήτε νοήσαντος τὸ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν γεγραμμένον μήτε κρῖναι δυναμένου ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τὸ βούλημα τῶν σοφῶν ἐκείνων ἀνδρῶν νομίζειν πρεσβεύεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν πλεῖον πίστεως μηδὲν ἐπαγγελλομένων τῆς πρὸς τὸν Χριστιανῶν λόγον· φέρε παραστήσωμεν ὅτι ἀνδράσιν οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτοις τῆς λογικῆς ἕνεκεν θεωρίας καὶ τῶν διαλεκτικῶν σκεμμάτων σφόδρα ἀπεμφαίνοντα λέλεκται. καὶ εἰ χρὴ μυχθίζειν ὡς ταπεινοὺς καὶ γραώδεις λόγους, ἐκείνους μᾶλλον χρὴ ἢ τοὺς ἡμετέρους. φασὶ δὴ οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς κατὰ περίοδον ἐκπύρωσιν τοῦ παντὸς γίνεσθαι καὶ ἑξῆς αὐτῇ διακόσμησιν, πάντ᾿ ἀπαράλλακτα ἔχουσαν ὡς πρὸς τὴν προτέραν διακόσμησιν. ὅσοι δ᾿ αὐτῶν ᾐδέσθησαν το δόγμα, ὀλίγην εἰρήκασι παραλλαγὴν καὶ σφόδρα βραχεῖαν γίνεσθαι κατὰ περίοδον τοῖς ἐπὶ τῆς πρὸ αὐτῆς περιόδου. οὗτοι δ᾿ οἱ ἄνδρες φασὶ τῇ ἑξῆς περιόδῳ τοιαῦτα ἔσεσθαι, καὶ Σωκράτην μὲν πάλιν Σωφρονίσκου υἱὸν καὶ Ἀθηναῖον ἔσεσθαι, καὶ τὴν Φαιναρέτην γημαμένην Σωφρονίσκῳ πάλιν αὐτὸν γεννήσειν. κἂν μὴ ὀνομάζωσιν οὖν τὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὄνομα, τὸ πρᾶγμά γε δηλοῦσιν, ὅτι Σωκράτης ἀπὸ σπερμάτων ἀρξάμενος ἀναστήσεται τῶν Σωφρονίσκου καὶ ἐν τῇ ὑστέρᾳ Φαιναρέτης διαπλασθήσεται καὶ ἀνατραφεὶς Ἀθήνῃσι φιλοσοφήσει, οἱονεὶ καὶ τῆς πρότερον φιλοσοφίας ἀνισταμένης καὶ ὁμοίως ἀπαραλλάκτου τῇ προτέρᾳ ἐσομένης. καὶ Ἄνυτος δὲ καὶ Μέλητος ἀναστήσονται πάλιν Σωκράτους κατήγοροι, καὶ ἡ ἐξ Ἀρείου πάγου βουλὴ καταδικάσεται τὸν Σωκράτην. τὸ δὲ τούτων γελοιότερον, τὰ ἀπαράλλακτα ἱμάτια τοῖς ὡς πρὸς τὴν προτέραν περίοδον Σωκράτης ἐνδύσεται, ἐν ἀπαραλλάκτῳ πενίᾳ καὶ ἀπαραλλάκτῳ πόλει ταῖς Ἀθήναις τῇ πρὸς τὴν προτέραν περίοδον ἐσόμενος. καὶ Φάλαρις μὲν τυραννήσει πάλιν, ὁ δὲ χάλκεος αὐτοῦ ταῦρος τῶν ἀπαραλλάκτων τῇ προτέρᾳ ἀνθρώπων περιόδῳ κατακριθέντων μυκήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς τῶν ἔνδον φωνῆς. Ἀλέξανδρός τε ὁ Φεραῖος πάλιν τυραννήσει, τὴν ἀπαράλλακτον ἔχων ὠμότητα τῇ προτέρᾳ καὶ τοὺς ἀπαραλλάκτους καταδικάζων ὡς καὶ τοὺς προτέρους. καὶ τί με δεῖ καταλέγειν τὸ περὶ τῶν τοιούτων δόγμα τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς πεφιλοσοφημένον καὶ μὴ γελώμενον ὑπὸ Κέλσου ἀλλὰ τάχα καὶ σεμνυνόμενον, ἐπεὶ δοκεῖ αὐτῷ ὁ Ζήνων τοῦ Ἰησοῦ εἶναι σοφώτερος;
pass_a_gloss: But since our [views] about resurrection, as room allowed (ἐγχωρέω), have been said in part (ἀπὸ τοῦ μέρους) for the present (for a treatise on resurrection has been composed (συντάσσω) by us elsewhere, having examined (ἐξετάζω) more fully the matters of the topic), now it is necessary, as is reasonable (εὔλογον), to deal with (διαλαμβάνω) the [words] of Celsus, who neither understood what is written among us nor was able to judge that one must not think the intention (βούλημα) of those wise men to be represented/championed (πρεσβεύω) by those professing (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) nothing more than faith toward the Christians' teaching (λόγος); come, let us show that by men not easily despised (εὐκαταφρόνητος, neg.) for the sake of logical theory (λογικὴ θεωρία) and dialectical inquiries (διαλεκτικὰ σκέμματα) very absurd things (ἀπεμφαίνω, ptc.) have been said. And if one must sneer (μυχθίζω) at stories as base (ταπεινός) and old-womanish (γραώδης), one must [sneer at] those rather than ours. The [men] from the Stoa (Στοά) say that by period (περίοδος) a conflagration (ἐκπύρωσις) of the all comes to be and next to it a world-ordering (διακόσμησις), having all things unvarying (ἀπαράλλακτα) as regards the former ordering. As many of them as were ashamed (αἰδέομαι) of the doctrine (δόγμα) have said a little variation (παραλλαγή) and very short comes to be by period, relative to the things in the period before it. These men say in the next period such things will be: Socrates again will be son of Sophroniscus and an Athenian, and Phaenarete, married (γαμέω) to Sophroniscus, will again beget (γεννάω) him. Even if they do not name the name of resurrection, they show the thing (πρᾶγμα) at least, that Socrates, beginning from seeds (σπέρματα) of Sophroniscus, will rise (ἀνίστημι), and will be formed (διαπλάσσω) in the womb (ὑστέρα) of Phaenarete, and brought up (ἀνατρέφω) at Athens will philosophise, as if also the former philosophy were rising and would be likewise unvarying with the former. And Anytus and Meletus will rise again accusers (κατήγοροι) of Socrates, and the council (βουλή) from the Areopagus will condemn (καταδικάζω) Socrates. More laughable (γελοῖος) than these: Socrates will put on (ἐνδύω) clothes (ἱμάτια) unvarying with those as of the former period, being in unvarying poverty (πενία) and in an unvarying city, Athens, as to the former period. And Phalaris will be tyrant (τυραννέω) again, and his bronze (χάλκεος) bull (ταῦρος), men unvarying with the former period having been condemned (κατακρίνω), will bellow (μυκάομαι) from the voice of those inside. And Alexander of Pherae will again be tyrant, having cruelty (ὠμότης) unvarying with the former and condemning the unvarying [men] as also the former. And why need I list (καταλέγω) the doctrine about such things philosophised (φιλοσοφέω) by those from the Stoa and not laughed at by Celsus but perhaps even revered (σεμνύνω), since Zeno seems to him wiser (σοφώτερος) than Jesus?

pass_b_english: What we hold about the resurrection has now been said in part, as far as room allowed for the present; for we have composed a work on the resurrection elsewhere, where we examined the questions of this subject at greater length. Now we must deal, as is reasonable, with what Celsus says. He has neither understood what is written among us nor been able to judge that the meaning of those wise men must not be thought to be represented by people who profess nothing more than faith in the Christians’ teaching.

Come, let us show that men who are not to be despised for their logical theory and their dialectical inquiries have said things that are wholly absurd; and if any teachings are to be sneered at as base old wives’ tales, it is theirs rather than ours.

The Stoics say that periodically a conflagration of the universe takes place, and after it a reordering of the world, with everything exactly the same as in the former ordering. Those of them who were ashamed of the doctrine have said that a slight and very small difference arises from cycle to cycle compared with what was in the cycle before. These men say that in the next cycle things will be as follows: Socrates will again be the son of Sophroniscus and an Athenian, and Phaenarete, married to Sophroniscus, will give birth to him again.

So even if they do not use the name of resurrection, they point to the thing itself: Socrates, starting from the seed of Sophroniscus, will rise again and be formed in the womb of Phaenarete, and having been brought up in Athens he will be a philosopher, as though his former philosophy also were rising again and would be just the same as before. Anytus and Meletus too will rise again as accusers of Socrates, and the council of the Areopagus will condemn Socrates. What is more laughable still, Socrates will put on clothes exactly the same as in the former cycle, and he will live in exactly the same poverty and in exactly the same city of Athens as in the former cycle. Phalaris will be a tyrant again, and his bronze bull will bellow with the voices of those inside it, men exactly the same as those condemned in the former cycle. Alexander of Pherae will be a tyrant again, with cruelty exactly the same as before, condemning men exactly the same as those he condemned before.
Why need I list the Stoics’ philosophical teaching on such matters? Celsus does not laugh at it, but perhaps even reveres it, since Zeno seems to him wiser than Jesus.
notes: The work on the resurrection Origen mentions is his lost treatise On the Resurrection. 'Those wise men' (τῶν σοφῶν ἐκείνων ἀνδρῶν) most likely means the wise writers of Scripture (such as Paul, just quoted), whose meaning simple believers do not represent; πρεσβεύεσθαι taken as 'represented' (also possible: 'upheld'). Origen's long protasis (Ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ ... λέλεκται) with the staged text's full stop before τὰ δὲ τοῦ Κέλσου is rendered as separate sentences. ἀπαράλλακτος (repeated for rhetorical effect) rendered 'exactly the same' throughout. Historical note: Socrates was tried by a popular court, not the Areopagus; Origen's wording is kept. Phalaris was tyrant of Acragas; Alexander of Pherae a fourth-century BC tyrant in Thessaly. The Stoic doctrine of conflagration and identical recurrence is reported, not quoted; no classical source cited inline. Zeno = Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoa; 'wiser than Jesus' is Origen's description of Celsus's view, not a quotation. Staged text has typo το for τὸ (δόγμα).
